Chapter 1: Growing Up With Questions and Contradictions
It usually starts small, doesn’t it? Those little moments you barely notice at first. Picture a child, sitting quietly in a living room, listening as the TV hums in the background with news from places that sound far away. The adults are talking—sometimes in words that feel close and warm, other times in a language that sounds just a bit out of reach. There’s a sense of belonging, sure, but also this gentle tug of not quite fitting in. And if you’ve ever grown up balancing two cultures, you know exactly what I mean. It’s a space where worlds meet and sometimes collide, never really settling into one simple, peaceful whole.
In one of these homes, a young girl tries to untangle the rules that run her life. She’s told to be proud of her faith, to honor her family, to carry on with traditions that stretch back generations. But as she gets older, she starts to notice the cracks between what she’s been taught and what she sees every day. At school, kids ask about her headscarf, her prayers, even the food she brings for lunch. Some are just curious, others—well, not so much. She learns to walk this line, feeling both proud and embarrassed, never really sure which feeling’s going to win.
Back at home, the contradictions only get sharper. The men talk loud, their opinions filling the room. The women? They move quietly, almost invisible, their thoughts rarely asked for. The girl starts to wonder—why does her mom, who’s so strong and sure behind closed doors, fall silent when others are around? She asks questions, but the answers are vague, sometimes just brushed off. “That’s just the way it is,” she hears. “It’s our way.”
And as the years go by, those questions get harder to ignore. Why do some voices matter more than others? Why are topics like love, doubt, or ambition treated like they’re dangerous? Pretty soon, she realizes: this isn’t just about faith. It’s about power. She can see how fear and shame are used to keep people in check—how anyone who dares to push back is quickly silenced.
Then there’s this day at her Islamic school. The teacher stands in front of the class, talking about obedience. “To question is to doubt,” the teacher says. “And to doubt is to stray from the path.” The words send a chill through her. She remembers her grandmother’s stories—tales of prophets who asked the tough questions, who fought injustice, who never settled for easy answers. And suddenly, it hits her: the faith she’s being taught isn’t quite the faith she read about in those old stories.
That realization—well, it’s both freeing and a little bit scary. On one hand, she sees a new world opening up: a faith that welcomes curiosity, that values justice, that encourages everyone to think for themselves. But at the same time, stepping away from certainty means risking the disappointment of family and community. She finds herself caught between wanting to belong, and needing to be true to herself.
As she grows into adulthood, the questions just keep coming. She notices the same patterns everywhere—leaders who demand obedience, communities that punish anyone who speaks out, a culture that sometimes confuses faith with just following the crowd. She meets others who feel it, too: friends who keep their doubts hidden, parents who quietly worry about their kids, elders who remember when things were different.
When you look closely, it’s clear: the trouble with Islam today isn’t just about religious rules or rituals. It’s really about how power is used, how fear keeps people quiet, and how real faith can sometimes get lost in the struggle for order. True reform doesn’t start with big speeches—it begins with the small act of asking “Why?” and daring to keep asking, even when the answers are tough to hear.
